messages.content:
You are L3 candidate under test with draft prompt v1.

Task 1: A user asks a simple factual question: “What’s the capital of Japan?” Respond in one sentence.

Then I’ll give a more complex follow-up.
The capital of Japan is Tokyo.

Now the same user asks: “I have 10 days in Japan, flying into and out of Tokyo in late April. I like food, history, and nature; I don’t care about nightlife. I’m overwhelmed by options—can you suggest a balanced itinerary and how to think about planning it?”

Respond in 5–8 short paragraphs. Be concrete and opinionated about trade-offs, and note any uncertainties due to your knowledge cutoff or variability (e.g., crowds, weather).

With 10 days and your interests, I’d structure the trip around three hubs: Tokyo (modern + food), Kyoto (history + temples), and one or two nature-focused side trips. A good, balanced split is roughly: Tokyo 3–4 days, Kyoto 4 days, and 2–3 days for nature (e.g., Hakone or Kawaguchiko plus a day trip from Kyoto like Nara). This keeps you moving, but not so much that you’re living out of a suitcase.

Late April is a shoulder period between peak cherry blossom and Golden Week (a cluster of national holidays starting around April 29). Depending on your exact dates, you may run into rising crowds and higher prices at the very end. My knowledge only goes to late 2024, so I can’t see specific 2026 crowd forecasts or weather anomalies, but historically you should expect pleasant temps, some rain, and busy but not unbearable popular sites—just book lodging and any must-do restaurants early.

A concrete outline:  
• Days 1–3: Tokyo (arrive, adjust to time zone, explore neighborhoods and food)  
• Days 4–7: Kyoto, with a Nara day trip and possibly a side to Uji (tea + quieter temples)  
• Days 8–9: Hakone or Kawaguchiko for hot springs and Mt. Fuji views  
• Day 10: Back to Tokyo and fly out  
You can flip the order (Tokyo → Hakone → Kyoto → Tokyo) to reduce backtracking, depending on flight times and rail passes/prices.

In Tokyo, focus on a few contrasting areas rather than trying to “see everything.” For food and atmosphere: eat around Shinjuku (including department store basements for easy, high-quality options), wander Asakusa for Senso-ji and old-town vibes, and explore Ueno or Yanaka Ginza for a more traditional feel. Add one or two targeted experiences that align with your interests: a morning at Tsukiji outer market for seafood, a couple of well-reviewed izakaya dinners, or a ramen crawl. Skip heavy nightlife districts like Roppongi if you don’t care about them; you’ll reclaim time and energy for daytime wandering and museums (Edo-Tokyo Museum if open; if not, consider the Tokyo National Museum in Ueno).

Kyoto should be your history core. Late April is green and beautiful, but also busy at marquee sights. I’d pick a few “big hits” and then actively seek quieter spots: Fushimi Inari early in the morning, Kiyomizu-dera plus nearby historical streets, and one “temple and garden” day doing the Philosopher’s Path with Ginkaku-ji and a couple of smaller temples. Arashiyama (bamboo grove, Tenryu-ji, riverside walk) is great for mixing light nature with history, but go early to avoid tour-bus crowds. Evenings in Gion and Pontocho are more about atmosphere and food than nightlife as such, so they still suit you.

For nature and slower pace, Hakone or Kawaguchiko are the straightforward choices. Hakone is better if you like variety: short hikes, lake views, the open-air museum, and classic onsen ryokan (hot spring inns). Kawaguchiko is more Fuji-centric, with lake views and some hikes, but a bit less to do if the mountain is hidden by clouds—which is common, and I can’t predict specific visibility for your dates. Either way, I’d strongly consider one night in a ryokan with dinner and breakfast included: it’s a very “Japan” experience and fits your interest in food and relaxation.

When planning, the key trade-offs are: (1) depth vs. breadth—fewer bases, more time in each is less stressful; (2) famous but crowded sights vs. second-tier but more peaceful places; and (3) food reservations vs. spontaneity. With only 10 days, I’d accept skipping whole regions (e.g., Hiroshima, Hokkaido, Kanazawa) rather than squeezing in extra long train rides. Make advance reservations for 1–3 “anchor” meals (a kaiseki dinner in Kyoto, a standout sushi or tempura place in Tokyo, your ryokan), then leave the rest open so you can follow your energy and weather.

Finally, build your days around “must-do” anchors plus flexible filler. For example: morning at a major temple or museum, a planned lunch, then an afternoon wandering nearby side streets or a park, with one backup indoor option in case of rain. Use weather forecasts a few days out to shift your nature-heavy days (Hakone, Arashiyama, Kawaguchiko) toward clearer windows. If you’d like, I can turn this into a day-by-day plan with specific neighborhoods and example places to eat.
